readerTitle: Which shop owner really owns more?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (철물점 두 곳, 인력 파견 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 대차대조표는 회사가 가진 것 전부에 대해 누가 먼저 청구권을 갖는지 보여주는 한 날짜의 사진이다. 소유주 몫은 빚을 다 갚고 남는 나머지일 뿐이다.
misconception: 자산이 많은 회사가 더 부자다. 자본(equity)은 통장에 있는 돈이다.

sources.text: 재무회계의 표준 개념 (자산 = 부채 + 자본, 복식부기)

factChecks.note: softwareNote의 선결제 구독(이연수익)은 부채로 기록된다는 일반 원칙만 언급. 자세한 내용은 FIN-11-04에서 다룸.

cards.title: Which shop owner really owns more?
body: Two hardware stores sit on the same street. Hal's has $500,000 of stock, cash and equipment. Mia's has $300,000.
Hal's store is bigger and busier. But that doesn't mean Hal owns more of it.

image.label: Two hardware shops side by side, one much larger
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 거리의 철물점 두 곳. 왼쪽은 크고 선반이 가득, 오른쪽은 작고 단정함. 큰 가게 뒤에 은행과 납품 트럭의 희미한 그림자가 걸쳐 있음. 실제 상표나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Who has more of the business that's truly theirs?
body: Hal owes his supplier $150,000 for stock and the bank $300,000 for a loan. Mia owes her supplier $50,000 and has no loan.
If both sold everything today at the recorded values and paid what they owe, who would walk away with more?

options.text: Hal. His store holds $200,000 more in assets
options.feedback: Size is easy to see, but much of Hal's stock was paid for with other people's money. Assets alone don't say who owns them.

options.text: Mia. She owes far less against what she has
options.feedback: Right. Mia keeps $250,000 after paying what she owes. Hal keeps $50,000. Next card shows the math.

options.text: You can't tell without last year's profit
options.feedback: Profit tells you how the year went and matters for the future. But this question is about what each owner holds today, and the numbers above already answer it.

cards.title: Hal's store on one day.
body: Mia's version is shorter: $300,000 − $50,000 = **$250,000**. Her store is smaller, but her stake is five times Hal's.

cards.title: The balance sheet
body: A **balance sheet** is a snapshot of a business on one date. It lists what the business owns (*assets*), what it owes (*liabilities*), and what's left for the owners (*equity*).
It always balances: **assets = liabilities + equity**. Every dollar of stuff was paid for either by someone the business owes or by the owners.
The income statement covers a period, like a year. The balance sheet covers a single moment.

image.label: A scale: assets on one side, liabilities plus equity on the other
image.brief: 균형 잡힌 저울 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 접시에 "Assets $500k"(현금, 재고, 선반 아이콘). 오른쪽 접시에 "Liabilities $450k"(큰 블록)와 "Equity $50k"(작은 블록)가 쌓여 있음. 저울은 정확히 수평.

cards.softwareNote: A software company that sells annual plans paid upfront gets the cash as an asset. It also records a liability, because it still owes a year of service to those customers.

cards.title: Every move touches two lines.
body: Because the sheet must balance, each event changes at least two places.
list: **Hal buys $20,000 of stock on credit:** stock up $20k, owed to supplier up $20k. His share doesn't change.
**He pays that supplier:** cash down $20k, owed down $20k. Still no change.
**He sells $1,000 of stock for $1,500:** stock down $1,000, cash up $1,500. His share grows by **$500**, the profit.
cards.callout: Only profit, losses, or owners putting money in or taking it out change the owner's share.

cards.title: Equity is not money in the bank.
body: Hal's share is $50,000, but that isn't a pile of cash. It's a leftover after subtracting debts from things like stock and shelves.
Those things are usually recorded at what they cost, not what they'd fetch today. Dusty stock that won't sell still counts at full price. Loyal customers and a good reputation don't appear at all.
So **equity is an accounting leftover**, not a price tag for the business.

cards.title: It's one day, and days can be picked.
body: A toy shop looks stuffed with stock and supplier bills on December 1, and lean on January 15. Neither date is wrong. Each shows only that moment.
A business can also tidy up right before the date, such as paying down a bill to look less indebted, then borrowing again next week.
Compare the same date year to year, and read the balance sheet next to the income and cash flow statements.

cards.title: Now it's a staffing agency.
body: You're about to sign a two-year deal with an agency that supplies your warehouse staff. Its balance sheet: assets $1.2M (cash $100k, clients owe it $1.1M). Liabilities: wages owed $200k, bank loan $900k. Equity: $100k.
What do you do before signing?

options.text: Sign. $1.2M in assets shows a solid firm
options.feedback: Most of those assets are other clients' unpaid bills, and most of them are matched by debt. The cushion is only $100k.

options.text: Ask how much of the $1.1M is overdue and when the loan is due
options.feedback: This tests whether the assets are real and whether the debts arrive before the cash. It takes one conversation and protects your workforce.

options.text: Ask only for last year's profit
options.feedback: Profit shows if the agency earns money. It won't show whether a late-paying client plus a loan deadline could leave your staff unpaid.

cards.title: Ask not just what a business has, but who it belongs to.
body: Assets minus what's owed equals the owners' share. A big business with a thin share can be more fragile than a small one with a thick share.
**Try it today:** list what your business owns and what it owes as of today. Subtract. Is the leftover what you expected?
